newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grain - Korea, Japan to buy despite rally.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Korea, Japan to buy despite rally.

text.p: Japan and South Korea will continue to buy wheat and barley near term despite the recent surge in wheat futures spurred by escalating concerns over U.S. crop losses caused by freezing weather, traders said on Monday.
Japan's Food Agency, the country's sole importer of wheat and barley, plans to buy 370,000 tonnes of wheat and 110,000 tonnes of barley this month.

"They're buying at a constant pace, and are likely to remain a constant buyer," a wheat trader in Japan said. "But it's possible that the agency (may) postpone some buying if the market remains bullish."
Traders in South Korea's major flour milling companies said they plan to buy more than 60,000 tonnes of U.S. No. 1 wheat for June/July shipment this week if prices remain firm.
"If wheat prices are expected to remain firm, we can no longer delay our purchases for nearby shipment," one said.

Cheiljedang Corp and Dongah Flour Mills Co Ltd will hold a joint tender for up to 40,000 tonnes of wheat for shipment in June while Daehan Flour Mills Co Ltd is expected to seek over 20,000 tonnes of wheat, company officials said.
South Korean companies were also said to be interested in two 50,000-tonne cargoes of feed wheat.
Taiwanese buyers are seen retendering for 68,000 tonnes of wheat for May/June delivery while buyers from the Philippines are likely to stay sidelined by high prices, dealers said.

U.S. wheat prices have soared with the July futures contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (COBT) hitting a 10-1/2 month session high of US$4.47 a bushel last Friday before settling 13-1/2 U.S. cents up on the day at $4.44-1/2 a bushel.
The July wheat contract on the exchange's Project A after hours trading system rose further on Monday by six U.S. cents to $4.50-1/2 a bushel at 0530 GMT.
The trade is now waiting for U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) report on the hard red winter wheat crop, due later on Monday, to indicate fresh market direction.
There was also concern in the trade about the dry weather affecting wheat farms in Europe, especially in France.
Concerns over the U.S. wheat crop have risen increased after floods inundated about 1.7 million acres of cropland in North Dakota.
The corn market will probably see more from Japanese buyers, who have already covered two thirds of their U.S. corn requirements for July-September shipment, traders said.
Corn premiums were quoted in Japan at about 92 to 93 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT May contract.
"Our memory of the corn market's price surges last year is still vivid, and (we) would likely to cover at a quicker pace this year," an official at a major Japanese feed maker said.

An official with Pan Ocean Shipping in South Korea said freight rates from the U.S. Pacific Northwest have fallen to $13.00-$14.00 a tonne from $14.50-$15.00 a tonne last week due to soft demand for nearby shipments of Panamax-sized cargo.
Rates from the U.S. Gulf for nearby shipments of Panamax cargoes were also seen falling to $23.00-$24.00 a tonne from $24.50-$25.00 a tonne last week.
